Global Competition Playbook: The Battle for Buyers & Sellers
LatAm eCommerce remains competitive, particularly in Brazil, while the investment backdrop acts as an underappreciated accelerant for the online retail shift. We see LatAm eCommerce as a US$220 billion market in 2025, representing 14.5% of retail sales. Penetration rose +140bps y/y, for a fourth consecutive year of accelerating gains as top online platforms improve convenience, selection, and speeds faster than offline retail innovates. Although often framed as a headwind, we see competition catalyzing TAM expansion. Namely, companies are racing to bring new buyers, sellers, and purchase occasions online, backed by capital investments (including logistics build-outs) and operating investments (including customer acquisition and buyer/seller subsidies). We see this continuing and forecast a +18% ex-FX / +13% USD CAGR for LatAm eCommerce volumes through 2029, reaching ~21% penetration, slightly below today's global average.
Proprietary survey data supports our growth outlook, demonstrating frequency gains despite still-nascent uptake of AI-enabled Agentic shopping tools. Purchase frequency gains stood out in our 8th AlphaWise Brazil & Mexico eCommerce survey (conducted November 2025). A sizable 59% of Brazil consumers reported a past-week online purchase, up +7pp y/y and marking survey highs; Mexico past-week penetration was 52%, in-line with prior highs. Uptake of Agentic Commerce tools that can further reduce online buying friction remains nascent, used by just 12% of Brazil consumers in the past 3 months (flat y/y). In our view, this indicates further runway for the online shift as AI-enabled roll-outs broaden. We see use of other AI tools as a leading indicator for eCommerce uptake: only 17% of Brazil consumers did not report using any GenAI tools over the past 3 months (-10pp y/y) and only 18% in Mexico (-9pp) reported no usage.
Looking to buyer competition, survey data shows a big-gettingbigger trend, with gains for Shopee and MELI in Brazil, and for Amazon and MELI in Mexico... In Brazil, Shopee (SE.N, covered by Divya Kothiyal) widened its lead as a top-3 purchase frequency destination, at 60% of consumers (+6pp y/y), while MELI rose to 47% (+3pp y/y). In Mexico, Amazon (AMZN.O, covered by Brian Nowak) was cited as a top-3 platform by 59% of consumers (+2pp y/y), while MELI at 51% narrowed the gap with a +4pp y/y increase. We see complementary strengths, with Shopee Brazil leading in clothing &
beauty, MELI in electronics & appliances, and Amazon in books. In Mexico, both top platforms have category breadth, while Amazon edged out MELI on most verticals and Walmex (WALMEX.MX) leads in grocery. For purchase drivers, MELI and Amazon surveyed aboveaverage in both countries on price, product quality, and service (i.e., delivery speeds & ease of returns). Shopee Brazil lagged only on perceived product quality, though with a +2pp y/y improvement in consumers very or somewhat satisfied on this metric (to 82%). MELI Brazil notably saw a +7pp improvement (to 79%) in satisfaction on delivery costs, which we attribute largely to the June '25 free shipping minimum reduction.
… while local platforms and cross-border operators saw declines, and TikTok Shop registered limited survey impact in its first year operating in the region. For local operators, in Brazil both Magazine Luiza (MGLU3.SA) and Casas Bahia (BHIA3.SA) posted a fourth year of declines as top-3 purchase destinations, broad-based across categories outside of Casas Bahia's increase in consumer electronics. In Mexico, Walmex declined for a second year albeit with gains in core grocery. For cross-border platforms, Temu (PDD.O, covered by Eddy Wang) in Mexico reverted -2pp y/y as a top-3 platform for 15% of consumers, while in Brazil it ranked at just 2%. AliExpress (BABA.N, covered by Gary Yu) declined to a similarly-modest 5% in Mexico and 4% in Brazil. In Mexico these platforms had slight favorable price perception but ranked below peers on other attributes; in Brazil perception was broadly below-peer. Temu's app momentum has slowed, and with a low-ticket focus we see market share under-indexing relative to app usage. For TikTok Shop, new to our survey this year following a Feb '25 launch in Mexico and May '25 in Brazil, the platform was cited as top-3 by just 5% of consumers in both countries. While early, todate we see social commerce as complementary to the traditional eCommerce marketplace model.
Looking to seller competition, our new multi-factor take rate tracking shows it is not trivial for merchants to determine which platform is better-priced to sell on… With seller competition increasingly in focus, we introduce a take rate tracker spanning MELI, Amazon, and Shopee in Brazil; MELI and Amazon in Mexico; and MELI in Argentina — seeking to gauge who has the most assertive sellerfacing offers (our take rate file can be shared upon request). Our major takeaway is Brazil take rate curves are converging, but finding

pockets of "value" is not trivial given core commissions can vary by category, and logistics fees by price point & weight. Further, certain platforms offer premium tiers that can include installment payments, greater visibility, and faster speeds. For platform-level insights, we highlight (1) Shopee Brazil changes announced Jan '26 furthered convergence, with most price points seeing increases, while buyer-facing PIX payment discounts (not captured in our analysis) are an offset. (2) Amazon Brazil's promotional packages (including logistics/fulfillment waivers and Sao Paulo seller fee waivers) drive substantial seller discounts, but with a temporary nature and multiple conditions. (3) MELI's policies are localized by market, with differences magnified at the lowest price points; Argentina screens highest, including shipping minimums and financing costs. More recent Brazil take rate discount policies center on ensuring favorably-priced supply on MELI’s platform.
… while for seller-facing services around fulfillment and Fintech tie-ins, MELI leads. Importantly, we believe seller competition is about more than price — including service levels, delivery speeds, and Fintech tie-ins. In logistics, MELI expanded its lead for fulfillment centers in Brazil, with 28 at YE25 versus Amazon at 15 (YE25) and Shopee at 6 currently, by our industry tracking. We see this gap widening with MELI's +50% y/y planned expansion (to 42 Brazil FCs) by YE26. As peers build and densify fulfillment networks, we see MELI's existing logistics footprint, overall market share, and '26 investment stance supporting a continued lead. We also see MELI leading regionwide on Fintech tie-ins, including ~US$65 billion of on-platform payment processing volumes in '25, a US$2 billion merchant credit portfolio, and 34% of monthly active sellers with credit (4Q25).
We continue to see MELI with a wide and expanding regional share lead, while Shopee gains in Brazil and Amazon in Mexico as longtail/local operators cede ground. In collaboration with Morgan Stanley global analysts, we update sizing estimates and forecasts for international platforms in LatAm, a unique resource as this data is not readily available. Speaking to MELI's scale lead region-wide, we see ~30% LatAm eCommerce share, similar to the next 10-largest operators combined; coupling favorable survey perception with continued investment, we see share nearing 40% in 2029. In Brazil, we forecast Shopee gaining ~6pp (to ~25%) through 2029 and MELI gaining ~10pp (to ~49%), with local operators and the long-tail ceding ground; volumes shift to marketplaces, including operators such as Casas Bahia that historically focused on own-platform sales. In Mexico, we see more of a two-player market, forecasting Amazon gaining ~5pp (to ~25%) through 2029, with MELI gaining ~12pp (to ~39%). We see cross-border operators Temu and AliExpress maintaining ~MSD% combined share in both Brazil and Mexico, absent signs of traction in localizing operations and moving upmarket from
the core low-ticket focus. We do not explicitly forecast TikTok Shop amid the early launch, while we estimate ~2% Brazil run-rate share exiting 2025.
Competition drives a range of outcomes for industry profitability, but our base case is that rationality holds. With investments including shipping and marketing for MELI, seller acquisition for Amazon, and fulfillment infrastructure for Shopee, market concerns center on costs of growth. In our bear case (race to the bottom), the presence of multiple international operators with the potential to fund LatAm losses via profitable operations elsewhere drives pressure to industry margins. We look out for sustained and escalating take rate cuts toward the lowest common denominator in our tracking file as evidence of this case playing out. In our base case (rational competition), companies invest behind buyer and seller acquisition, including promotional periods and new category/capability build-outs, with efficiency gains re-invested selectively into faster speeds or lower prices. We see major LatAm operators' investment approach falling in this category. MELI's scale makes the platform difficult to displace, potentially preventing others from pursuing market share at any cost. In our bull case (monetization in-focus), select participants pare back LatAm eCommerce investments as promotional intensity does not yield sufficient ROI. This enables leading operators to pursue greater monetization of assets such as fulfillment infrastructure, acting as a tailwind for margins.
How to play it? With a Commerce margin bear case appearing priced in, we see outsized risk-reward for OW-rated MELI. Brazil upside potential is material for SE, relatively smaller for other international platforms. Our MELI base case Commerce margins remain below '23/'24 levels (of EBIT ~2% of GMV, by our estimate) through the next 3 years, with longer-term expansion from scale gains, logistics efficiencies, and advertising monetization. Our "what's in the price" DCF sensitivity shows the stock pricing Commerce EBIT margins near our bear case (<1% of GMV) for an extended period, and consolidated margins staying near FY25 levels in perpetuity. This appears overly punitive, in our view, supporting an outsized risk-reward skew. Elsewhere in LatAm we are UW-rated on MGLU3 and BHIA3 in Brazil and WALMEX in Mexico (downgraded in January), seeing a need to invest in digital capabilities but with more limited TAMs given category-specific strength. For SE, Divya Kothiyal and team believe Brazil will be a key growth and profit driver for Shopee, with AlphaWise data supporting the thesis of further share gains for Shopee in Brazil. For detail, see the companion note Shopee's Samba: Fueling the Momentum. LatAm can be a highergrowth market, albeit less impactful to consolidated results, for international platforms AMZN,PDD,BABA. Industry Growth Outlook: Investments Power Penetration Gains
LatAm eCommerce Model
2025 marked a third year of accelerating penetration gains for LatAm eCommerce (reaching 14.5%), and we look for +13% USD CAGR with penetration reaching 21% in 2029E. Moving past pandemic-era distortions, LatAm eCommerce penetration increased +120bps in 2024 and +140bps in 2025, accelerating from +70bps on average in '21-'23. We see a secular shift to digital commerce, continued investments in logistics/ selection/service at the company level, and reduced friction from adoption of AI in eCommerce (including Agentic offerings which are currently nascent in LatAm). With these trends continuing to take hold, and outpacing the rate of innovation across our LatAm physical retail coverage, we look for penetration gains to continue. We forecast +160bps average increases through 2029, reaching 21% ( Exhibit 22 ), similar to where the global average stands today. Combined with top-down support from interest rate easing cycles ( Exhibit 23 ) and a potential LatAm Spring bull case (see Morgan Stanley BluePaper), we forecast a +13% USD CAGR for LatAm eCommerce volumes (+18% in local currencies) through 2029.
Exhibit 22: We forecast LatAm eCommerce growing at a +13% USD CAGR between 2025 and 2029, with support from penetration which has been inflecting upward…

Brazil specifically saw a notable inflection to +200bps of penetration gains (and +21% y/y growth) as companies invest behind service & subsidies, and we expect this trend to continue in 2026. Multiple top platforms invested behind Brazil eCommerce in 2025, further powering the share shift online as physical-first operators contended with pressure from a high-rates backdrop (Brazil SELIC peaking at 15%). MELI reduced its free shipping minimum to R$19, accelerated customer acquisition spending, invested behind new verticals (including 1P & cross-border), and continued to build out service-driven moats around fulfillment density, and Commerce/Fintech loyalty. Shopee similarly invested behind logistics speeds and service levels, and Amazon made a push for fulfillment density with fee waivers for sellers entering its network. These initiatives came with margin pressure (evident in MELI's Brazil contribution margin contraction in '25), but the improved online value proposition furthered Brazil's eCommerce shift and supported share gain versus local platforms with less investment capacity. We expect an elevated investment stance to persist into 2026, but with corresponding growth. We forecast Brazil eCommerce growing +22% y/y with +250bps of penetration gains to 19.9% in 2026, with a +17% CAGR reaching 26% penetration in 2029 ( Exhibit 24 ). With support from AlphaWise survey data and our bottom-up company forecasts detailed further inside, we see penetration gains broad-based across categories ( Exhibit 25 ).

Looking to other key markets for the region, we look for a steady growth backdrop in Mexico and see Argentina benefitting from the ongoing macro normalization agenda. For Mexico, the market has seen steady underlying trends in recent years, with lower volatility in the competitive and rates/macro backdrops when compared to Brazil. We look for +18% eCommerce growth in MXN for 2026E (+23% in 2025), with a +16% CAGR through 2029E including ~7pp of penetration gains (to 24%); see Exhibit 26 . For Argentina, a reform path continued throughout 2025, with exit rate inflation of ~30% y/y versus >200% in 2024, along with near-convergence between official and unofficial FX rates. The macro backdrop has supported renewed investment in the country which can drive forward eCommerce growth, in our view. This includes MELI's opening of new fulfillment centers and launch of an Argentina credit card, while reduced import and capital restrictions have further opened a market for cross-border eCommerce in the country. We look for Argentina eCommerce to grow +44% ex-FX in 2026E, with penetration +150bps y/y to 18%, reaching 23% in 2029E ( Exhibit 27 ).

Buyers In-Focus — AlphaWise Survey Data
While Brazil and Mexico remain multi-player eCommerce markets, our AlphaWise survey (conducted in November 2025) shows frequency share concentrating in 2-3 top platforms by country. We asked consumers to rank the top three online retailers from which they purchase most frequently; results are shown in Exhibit 28 for Brazil and Exhibit 29 for Mexico. In Brazil, Shopee led, cited as a top-3 platform by 60% of respondents, with 37% ranking the platform as number one. Shopee was followed by MELI (47%), and Amazon (37%), then with a sharp step-down to 15% or less for remaining Brazil-based and cross-border platforms. Mexico showed slightly less concentration, with Amazon cited as a top-three platform by 59% of consumers, and number one by 34%. Amazon was followed by MELI (51%) and Walmex (36%), while there were more operators than Brazil in the ~10-20% range. TikTok Shop, new to our survey this year, was a top-3 platform for just 5% of consumers in Brazil & Mexico, indicating that social commerce uptake remains early-stage.

Brazil trends echo the concentration narrative, with Shopee and MELI frequency share increasing y/y, while other major platforms (including Amazon) saw decreases. In Exhibit 30 we compare the survey results for frequent purchase destination in 2025 versus prior years. Shopee widened its lead, as a top-3 purchase frequency destination for 60% of consumers (+6pp y/y), while MELI at 47% increased +3pp. Conversely, Amazon was a modest -1pp to 37%, reversing the recent years' trend of new highs. Declines were even greater for the next tier of platforms including Shein, Magazine Luiza, and Americanas. Consumers reported consistency between most-frequent and highest-spending platforms, contrary to our expectation of divergence based on average price point. New to our survey this year we asked consumers which online retailers "they spend the most on," in addition to our long-standing question of which retailers they "purchase from most frequently." As shown in Exhibit 34 for Brazil and Exhibit 35 for Mexico there was a very high correlation between responses for these two questions. This was contrary to our view that lower-ticket cross-border platforms (i.e., Temu) would over-index for frequency but under-index for spending, with the reverse for durable goods retailers such as Casas Bahia and Magazine Luiza. We continue to see different purchasing use cases by platforms, but our survey shows that consumers equate buying frequency with spending in a fairly direct manner.

Top platforms show increasing breadth at the category level, while Shopee over-indexed for softlines and MELI hard goods; these two platforms had y/y gains, while most other operators declined. In Exhibit 36 we show the proportion of survey respondents that bought a certain merchandise category from each operator over the past 12 months, with y/y changes in Exhibit 37 . Among top operators, Shopee had the greatest proportion of consumers who purchased clothing/shoes/accessories (at 57%), home furnishings/accessories (58%), athletic apparel (49%), and beauty/personal care items (51%) on the platform. MELI led for mobile devices/accessories (at 52%) and consumer electronics (54%), also moving into the top spot for large appliances (42%) and home improvement (57%). Amazon led for books (69%) and showed breadth across categories. At Magazine Luiza and Casas Bahia, we continue to see an over-indexing toward appliances and electronics. When considering trends versus last year, Shopee showed gains (led by beauty), as did MELI (led by electronics & beauty), while other major platforms declined.

Demographics and Perception
Digging in on platform demographics, Shopee Brazil over-indexes for younger consumers and MELI for Class A; in Mexico, Amazon overindexes for higher-income cohorts, with MELI more balanced. In Exhibit 40 we break down the Brazil eCommerce purchase frequency data by age cohort; in Exhibit 41 by socioeconomic class; Exhibit 42 and Exhibit 43 show these trends for Mexico. In Brazil, Shopee led for all age cohorts ex-55+, while over-indexing for younger consumers (where its y/y gains were most notable). Shopee showed breadth by socio-economic class, retaining the widest lead in Class C where 63% ranked the platform as a top-three destination (MELI 45%). MELI over-indexed for Class A consumers while both MELI and Shopee were cited as a top-three destination by 57% in Brazil's Class A. We see Amazon balanced by age in Brazil, whereas in Mexico the platform over-indexes toward older consumers and Classes A & B. MELI in Mexico has balance across age and income demographics. Versus a simple take rate plus logistics fee model, we note that pricing structures have become increasingly complex. Temu LatAm Outlook
Temu’s original fully-entrusted model was built around ultra-low prices, centralized on cross-border supply, and aggressive traffic acquisition, supported by broad free-shipping and returns policies. That playbook helped the platform scale rapidly across global markets, including Brazil and Mexico.
However, in Brazil in particular, the economics of cross-border eCommerce have become less favorable under the Remessa Conforme regime, which requires taxes to be collected at checkout for qualifying platforms and changed the tax treatment of imported parcels beginning August 2024. Those changes have increased the pressure on low-ticket cross-border models and raised the strategic importance of local inventory, local sellers, and faster domestic fulfillment. In that context, Temu has been expanding its semi-entrusted model and local-to-local model, which allows sellers with local inventory to fulfill more directly and reduce delivery friction; in Brazil, local-inventory products have been advertised with delivery as fast as two business days. Temu is moving from being primarily a price-led cross-border platform toward a model that increasingly combines low prices, local inventory, and faster fulfillment.
Our model still sees Temu as a relevant but secondary player in LatAm commerce: we estimate Mexico market share at ~3.1% in 2025, rising to ~3.9% by 2029, and Brazil at ~1.2% in 2025, rising to ~2.2% by 2029. In other words, LatAm matters for Temu’s global traffic footprint, but today it still fits better as an incremental GMV contributor than as a market where Temu is reshaping competitive structures at the high end.
